title: Sport-Induced Modulation of the Endocannabinoid System in Adolescents With and Without Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder
summary:
Background
Some adolescents develop Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) after experiencing very stressful or traumatic events. PTSD can strongly affect daily life and reduce social and emotional well-being. Although psychotherapeutic treatments are available, there is currently no approved medication specifically for adolescents with PTSD. In addition, trauma-focused therapies can be lengthy and emotionally challenging for young people.
The biological causes of PTSD are not yet fully understood. Because of this, there are still no targeted treatments that directly address the underlying neurobiological mechanisms of the disorder.
One system that may play an important role is the endocannabinoid system. This natural system in the body helps regulate fear, stress, and emotions. A specific messenger substance called anandamide appears to be important: higher levels of anandamide have been linked to better “extinction” of fear responses. For this reason, influencing the endocannabinoid system is being discussed as a possible new approach for treating psychiatric conditions.
It is also known that anandamide levels in the blood reliably increase after physical exercise. Studies in adults with PTSD have shown that exercise, when added to trauma-focused therapy, can have positive effects.
However, we still know little about the biological processes behind these benefits—especially how the endocannabinoid system changes in the short term during and after physical activity. This gap in knowledge is even larger for adolescents, whose endocannabinoid system is still undergoing important developmental changes during puberty.
Based on this, we assume that the endocannabinoid system may play a role both in vulnerability to traumatic experiences and as a potential target for future treatments.

Research Question
We aim to find out how certain naturally occurring messenger substances of the endocannabinoid system change during and after physical activity in adolescents. We also want to understand whether these changes differ between adolescents with and without PTSD.

Methods
A total of 96 adolescents will take part in the study: half with PTSD and half without. All participants will complete a 30-minute exercise session, and blood samples will be taken at several time points. This allows us to measure how endocannabinoid levels change over time. In addition, the adolescents and their parents will complete questionnaires about life events, mood, and health.

interventions.name:
Open-Label Exercise Intervention (30 minutes)
Moderate physical activity targeting 70–75 % of the individual’s maximum heart rate.

Participants: Adolescents aged 14–18 years

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Ages 14 to 18
Sufficient knowledge of German
Written informed consent from participants (and, if under 16, from their legal guardians)
Group 1 – Patients with PTSD
Diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) according to clinical diagnosis
Currently receiving outpatient or inpatient treatment at the Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry/Psychotherapy, University Hospital Ulm
Willingness to participate in the standardized sports intervention and examinations
Group 2 – Healthy control subjects
No history of trauma, verified using the CATS-2 questionnaire (Child and Adolescent Trauma Screen)
No psychiatric abnormalities, verified by the SCID-I screening
Healthy, i.e., no neurological or mental illnesses
Exclusion criteria:
Current or recurrent neurological or psychiatric disorder (for control group)
Schizophrenic spectrum disorder
Positive urine test for THC-COOH or cannabis/CBD use within the last 6 months
Organic brain disorder
Severe physical illness
Acute substance use disorder
